analysis.one_liner: Writes a 'no net loss' national policy for wetlands into law and requires permits and compensation before wetlands can be destroyed.
analysis.headline: The Wetlands Stewardship Act of 1991 got one subcommittee hearing in November 1991 and then died in committee, never reaching a House floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it national policy that the country loses no more wetlands overall, and would require anyone who drains, digs up, or floods a wetland to get a federal permit and replace what they destroy, either by restoring wetlands or buying credits in a new wetlands 'mitigation bank.' It also offers landowners help and incentives to keep wetlands intact, lets states take over permitting under approved plans, and exempts ongoing farming, forestry done to state standards, and certain mining. Congress never voted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who depend on what wetlands provide: flood protection, cleaner water, fish and waterfowl habitat, and groundwater recharge. The bill's findings note the country had already lost over half its wetlands and was losing roughly 300,000 acres a year [S3]. Small property owners get specific relief, including a hardship appeal path for home construction affecting under three acres [S2]. States, local governments, and private landowners would receive federal grants, mapping, and technical assistance for conservation planning [S2].

how_it_helps.text: Writes a national 'no net loss' policy into the Clean Water Act: no overall loss of the remaining wetland base, plus restoration and creation to grow it back [S2].
Expands the permitting program so that dredging, excavation, channelization, draining, or flooding of wetlands all require a permit, not just dumping fill [S2].
Requires permit holders to avoid, minimize, and then compensate for wetland losses, with mitigation made an enforceable permit condition and monitored for effectiveness [S3].
Creates a wetlands mitigation banking system so that offsets are credentialed, accounted for, and geographically restricted rather than ad hoc promises [S3].

Gives small landowners a hardship appeal: for home construction or minor repairs affecting under three acres, a longtime owner can get the permit or reduced mitigation if denial would cause significant financial hardship [S2].

Provides federal grants, mapping, and technical help for state and local wetlands conservation planning, plus a program assisting private landowners to conserve wetlands and develop non-degrading economic uses [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Developers, mining companies, and other businesses that would face new permit requirements and mitigation costs before draining or altering wetlands. Farmers, timber operators, aquaculture operations, and aggregate or clay miners get carve-outs, but the carve-outs come with conditions like state-approved best management practices or reclamation bonding [S2]. Federal taxpayers fund the mapping, grants, and state plan assistance.

drawbacks.text: The regulatory net widens: activities like draining and flooding that previously escaped Section 404 would need permits, adding cost, delay, and compliance burdens for property owners and small businesses [S2].

The bill's own wetland definition excludes areas saturated fewer than 14 consecutive days in the growing season and prior-converted cropland, which could shrink protection compared with existing practice [S3].
The exemptions carry real loopholes: silviculture done under state best management practices is exempt outright, and ongoing aquaculture is exempt regardless of wetland impact [S2].

Mitigation banking lets destruction in one place be paid for by restoration elsewhere, and restored wetlands often underperform the natural ones they replace; the bill itself requires a report evaluating whether the system actually works [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: stronger wetland protection in exchange for new permitting costs and paperwork, with the heaviest burdens falling on commercial development. The bill tries to soften that with hardship appeals for small owners, state takeover options, and landowner assistance, but its exemptions for forestry, mining, and existing aquaculture are broad enough that critics could fairly call them gaps in the no-net-loss promise. On balance the design leans toward protecting a public resource while paying private parties to cooperate rather than simply prohibiting destruction.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in two House committees and their subcommittees, got one hearing in November 1991, and was never reported out or voted on before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Lindsay Thomas of Georgia introduced the bill on May 20, 1991, joined by nine other original sponsors, and it drew 15 cosponsors including 3 Republicans [S3][S4].
It was referred jointly to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries Committee and the Public Works and Transportation Committee, then split among three subcommittees [S5].
Executive comments were requested from USDA, Interior, the Army Corps of Engineers, and EPA in May 1991 [S5].
A subcommittee hearing was held on November 21, 1991, but no markup, committee vote, or floor action ever followed [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993, with the bill never reported out of committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses and landowners who drain or develop wetlands kept operating under the older, narrower Section 404 rules, with no new permit triggers, no compensation requirements, and no no-net-loss mandate. Roughly 300,000 acres of wetlands a year continued to disappear, per the bill's own findings, at a cost borne by people downstream and the public [S3].

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wetland developers kept the old loose rules

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan from the start: 12 Democrats and 3 Republicans cosponsored, and the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would extend permit requirements to draining, excavation, and flooding of wetlands and require compensating for losses, raising costs for projects that destroy wetlands. Those costs are the flip side of the flood control and water quality benefits wetlands provide to the public.

Drained and cropped cropland predating the bill is excluded from the wetland definition, and landowners get hardship appeals and a federal assistance program for conservation and non-degrading economic uses. But drainage changes beyond that face new permitting.

Normal silviculture conducted under state-approved best management practices would be expressly exempt from permitting, locking in forestry's operating freedom in wetlands at the cost of whatever wetlands that work degrades.
Mining would be exempt if conducted under a permit requiring reclamation within five years and a bond, a carve-out that lets mining proceed in wetlands in exchange for promised restoration.

The bill creates a formal credit system in which anyone who creates or restores wetlands earns credits that developers must buy to offset destruction, establishing a new revenue stream for restoration businesses. Public benefit and industry revenue rise together, though the credit system permits destruction in one place paid for by restoration elsewhere.

industries.industry: Commercial and recreational fisheries and waterfowl interests
industries.note: Wetlands are habitat for migratory birds, endangered species, and commercial and recreational fisheries; slowing the loss of 300,000 acres a year directly serves these users.
